claim: UNC-4 homeobox protein and its corepressor UNC-37/Groucho have a novel role in tiled synaptic patterning of the cholinergic motor neurons in Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: Here we identify a novel role for UNC-4 homeobox protein and its corepressor UNC-37/Groucho, in tiled synaptic patterning of the cholinergic motor neurons in Caenorhabditis elegans.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data showing synaptic tiling defects in unc-4 and unc-37 mutants.

claim: unc-4 is not required during neurogenesis but is required in the postmitotic neurons for proper synapse patterning.
source: We show that unc-4 is not required during neurogenesis but is required in the postmitotic neurons for proper synapse patterning.
evidence: This is supported by temporal knockdown experiments using temperature-sensitive mutants and the AID system showing that embryonic knockdown of unc-4 does not cause synaptic tiling defects, while postembryonic knockdown does.

claim: unc-37 is required in both developing and postmitotic neurons for proper synapse patterning.
source: In contrast, unc-37 is required in both developing and postmitotic neurons.
evidence: This is supported by temporal degradation experiments showing that both embryonic and postembryonic degradation of UNC-37 cause synaptic tiling defects.

claim: The synaptic tiling defects of unc-4 mutants are suppressed by bar-1/β-catenin mutation.
source: The synaptic tiling defects of unc-4 mutants are suppressed by bar-1/β-catenin mutation, which positively regulates the expression of ceh-12/HB9.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that bar-1(ga80) partially suppressed the synaptic tiling defect of unc-4 and unc-37 mutants.

claim: Ectopic ceh-12 expression partly underlies the synaptic tiling defects of unc-4 and unc-37 mutants.
source: Ectopic ceh-12 expression partly underlies the synaptic tiling defects of unc-4 and unc-37 mutants.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that ectopic expression of ceh-12 in DA neurons causes synaptic tiling defects, and that weak ectopic expression of ceh-12 is observed in unc-4 and unc-37 mutants.

claim: UNC-4 and UNC-37 regulate synapse pattern formation through inhibiting the canonical Wnt signaling pathway.
source: Our results reveal a novel postmitotic role of neuronal cell fate determinants in synapse pattern formation through inhibiting the canonical Wnt signaling pathway.
evidence: This is supported by genetic interaction data showing that bar-1/β-catenin mutation suppresses unc-4 and unc-37 synaptic tiling defects.

claim: The LIM homeobox transcription factor Isl1 determines cholinergic neuronal cell fates in the mice and chick spinal cord and hindbrain.
source: For example, a conserved LIM (LIN-11, Isl-1, MEC-3) homeobox transcription factor Isl1 determines cholinergic neuronal cell fates in the mice and chick spinal cord and hindbrain (Cho et al., 2014; Ericson et al., 1992; Liang et al., 2011; Pfaff et al., 1996; Tsuchida et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The Drosophila homolog of the vertebrate Isl1, islet, specifies motor neurons and interneurons in the ventral nerve cord.
source: Similarly, the Drosophila homolog of the vertebrate Isl1, islet, specifies motor neurons and interneurons in the ventral nerve cord (Thor and Thomas, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The HB9/MNR2 transcription factor is required for the differentiation and specification of motor neurons in chick and mice.
source: Furthermore, the HB9/MNR2 transcription factor is required for the differentiation and specification of motor neurons in chick and mice (Arber et al., 1999; Tanabe et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In C. elegans, MEC-3 and UNC-86 function cooperatively to specify the glutamatergic mechanosensory neurons.
source: In Caenorhabditis elegans, MEC-3 and UNC-86, which are LIM and POU (Pit-1/Oct1/2/UNC-86) homeobox proteins, respectively, function cooperatively to specify the glutamatergic mechanosensory neurons (Duggan et al., 1998; Finney et al., 1988; Way and Chalfie, 1988; Xue et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Many neuronal cell fate determinants are continuously expressed in postmitotic neurons.
source: Interestingly, many neuronal cell fate determinants are continuously expressed in postmitotic neurons (Deneris and Hobert, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Neuronal cell fate determinants are crucial for the neuronal maturation and maintenance of the respective cell fates.
source: Consistent with this sustained expression, several studies have shown that neuronal cell fate determinants are crucial for the neuronal maturation and maintenance of the respective cell fates.
evidence: This is supported by subsequent examples and citations in the text.

claim: The ETS domain transcription factor PET-1 is continuously expressed and controls the neuronal maturation of serotonergic neurons via controlling the expression of Engrailed 1.
source: For example, the ETS (Erythroblast Transformation Specific) domain transcription factor PET-1, which determines the serotonergic neuronal fates in the Raphe nuclei of the brainstem of mice, is continuously expressed (Hendricks et al., 1999) and controls the neuronal maturation of serotonergic neurons via controlling the expression of the neuronal maturation factor, Engrailed 1 (Wyler et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In C. elegans, UNC-3 is required for both specification and maintenance of the cholinergic motor neuron identities.
source: In C. elegans, the COE (Collier/Olf/EBF) type transcription factor, UNC-3, is required for both specification and maintenance of the cholinergic motor neuron identities (Kerk et al., 2017; Kratsios et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: UNC-86 and its mammalian ortholog BRN3A are required for the maintenance of the cell fates of several sensory neurons in C. elegans and the medial habenular neurons in mice.
source: The POU homeobox protein UNC-86 and its mammalian ortholog, BRN3A, are required for the maintenance of the cell fates of several sensory neurons in C. elegans and the medial habenular neurons in the diencephalon of mice (Serrano-Saiz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Drosophila HB9 is required in a subset of motor neurons and serotonergic interneurons for axon pathfinding and target specificity.
source: For example, Drosophila HB9 is required in a subset of ventrally projecting motor neurons and the serotonergic EW1, EW2, and EW3 interneurons for axon pathfinding and target specificity (Odden et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In unc-55 mutants, VD GABAergic motor neurons innervate the dorsal body wall muscles instead of the ventral body wall muscles due to ectopic expression of DD neuron-specific genes.
source: In C. elegans, in the mutants of unc-55, which encodes an ortholog of COUP-TF (chicken ovalbumin upstream promoter transcription factor), the ventrally innervating D-class (VD) GABAergic motor neurons innervate the dorsal body wall muscles instead of the ventral body wall muscles, due to the ectopic expression of the genes which are normally expressed only in the dorsally innervating D-class (DD) neurons (Howell et al., 2015; Shan et al., 2005; Zhou and Walthall, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In unc-3 mutants, the AVA interneurons lose the majority of synaptic connections with genuine targets and form ectopic synaptic connections with unidentified neurons.
source: In unc-3 mutants, the AVA interneurons lose the majority of the synaptic connections with the genuine targets and, in turn, form ectopic synaptic connections with unidentified neurons (Pereira et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Little is known about the postmitotic roles of neuronal cell fate determinants in neuronal wiring.
source: While functions of neuronal cell fate determinants in neuronal wiring and synaptic specificity have been identified, little is known about the postmitotic roles of neuronal cell fate determinants in neuronal wiring.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: UNC-4 specifies the ventral and dorsal A-type cholinergic motor neurons by repressing the alternative B-type neuronal fates in C. elegans.
source: The paired-type homeobox transcription factor, UNC-4, specifies the ventral and dorsal A-type cholinergic motor neurons (VAs and DAs) by repressing the alternative B-type neuronal fates (VBs and DBs) in C. elegans (Kerk et al., 2017; Kratsios et al., 2012; Winnier et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The repression of B-type fates requires the physical interaction between UNC-4 and UNC-37 to repress the expression of B-type-specific genes.
source: The repression of the B-type fates requires the physical interaction between UNC-4 and the Groucho-like transcriptional corepressor, UNC-37, to repress the expression of B-type-specific genes such as acr-16/nicotinic acetylcholine receptor and acr-5/acetylcholine receptor α-like subunit (Kerk et al., 2017; Winnier et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Loss of unc-4 and unc-37 does not alter the morphology of A-type motor neurons but results in altered connectivity from upstream command interneurons.
source: While the loss of unc-4 and unc-37 and the subsequent ectopic expression of B-type genes does not alter the morphology of A-type motor neurons, this results in the altered connectivity of the A-type motor neurons from the upstream command interneurons (Miller et al., 1992; White et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In wild-type animals, VA motor neurons receive presynaptic input from AVA command interneurons.
source: In wild-type animals, the VA motor neurons receive presynaptic input from the AVA command interneurons (White et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In unc-4 and unc-37 mutants, VA neurons form synaptic connections with AVB command interneurons instead of AVA interneurons.
source: However, in the loss of function mutants of unc-4 and unc-37, the VA neurons do not form synaptic connections with the AVA interneurons but instead form synaptic connections with the AVB command interneurons, which normally innervate the VB motor neurons (Miller et al., 1992; White et al., 1992; Winnier et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: unc-4 is required for proper AVA>VA connectivity primarily in the late first larval (L1) stage when the VA neurons are born.
source: Temporal knockdown experiments using a temperature-sensitive mutant of unc-4 showed that it is required for proper AVA>VA connectivity, primarily in the late first larval (L1) stage when the VA neurons are born, suggesting that this miswiring is likely due to the partial cell fate transformation of the A-type motor neurons to the B-type motor neurons (Miller et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Knockdown of unc-4 at L2-L3 also caused partial AVA>VA wiring defect, suggesting that unc-4 is required after the AVA>VA wiring completes.
source: However, the knockdown of unc-4 at L2-L3 also caused partial AVA>VA wiring defect, suggesting that unc-4 is also required after the AVA>VA wiring completes.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: unc-4 functions in the maintenance of AVA>VA synaptic connection.
source: This observation implies that unc-4 also functions in the maintenance of AVA>VA synaptic connection (Miller et al., 1992).
evidence: This is an inference based on previous experimental observations cited in the text.

claim: Drosophila Unc-4 promotes cholinergic fate and inhibits GABAergic fate during development.
source: Recent work in Drosophila has identified the role of Unc-4 to promote cholinergic fate and to inhibit GABAergic fate during development (Lacin et al., 2020), suggesting a conserved role of unc-4 in neuronal cell fate specification.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: DA neurons exhibit a unique 'tiled' synaptic innervation pattern, in which the synaptic domain of a DA neuron does not overlap with those from the neighboring DA neurons.
source: DA neurons exhibit a unique 'tiled' synaptic innervation pattern, in which the synaptic domain of a DA neuron does not overlap with those from the neighboring DA neurons (White et al., 1976; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Interaxonal interaction between DA8 and DA9 mediated by Semaphorin–Plexin signaling establishes the synaptic tiling of DA8 and DA9.
source: Previously, we have shown that the interaxonal interaction between two DA neurons (DA8 and DA9) mediated by Semaphorin–Plexin signaling establishes the synaptic tiling of DA8 and DA9 (Chen et al., 2018; Mizumoto and Shen, 2013a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: In unc-4 and unc-37 mutants, the tiled synaptic innervation between DA8 and DA9 is severely disrupted.
source: In the loss of function mutants of unc-4 and unc-37, we show that the tiled synaptic innervation between DA8 and DA9 is severely disrupted, similar to the mutants of Semaphorin-Plexin signaling components.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: unc-4(e120) null mutants show significant overlap between the DA8 and DA9 synaptic domains.
source: In unc-4(e120) null mutants, we found significant overlap between the DA8 and DA9 synaptic domains: the synapses of DA8 and DA9 are intermingled in the region of overlap (Figure 1C,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and quantified in Figure 1E.

claim: unc-37(e262) hypomorphic mutants exhibited significant overlap between the DA8 and DA9 synaptic domains.
source: Similar to unc-4, hypomorphic mutants of unc-37(e262), which carry a single amino acid substitution (H539Y) (Pflugrad et al., 1997), exhibited significant overlap between the DA8 and DA9 synaptic domains, indicating that unc-37 is also required for synaptic tiling (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and quantified in Figure 1E, and citation to previous literature.

claim: unc-4(e120) did not enhance the synaptic tiling defects of unc-37(e262).
source: Moreover, unc-4(e120) did not enhance the synaptic tiling defects of unc-37(e262) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: unc-4 and unc-37 function as a transcriptional repressor complex in the A-type motor neurons.
source: This result is consistent with the fact that unc-4 and unc-37 function as a transcriptional repressor complex in the A-type motor neurons (Winnier et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: UNC-4 physically interacts with UNC-37 via its carboxy-terminal Engrailed-like repressor (eh1) domain.
source: UNC-4 physically interacts with UNC-37 via its carboxy-terminal Engrailed-like repressor (eh1) domain (Winnier et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: unc-4(e26) mutants, which carry a missense mutation in the eh1 domain, show severe synaptic tiling defects.
source: Similar to unc-4(e120) null mutants, we observed severe synaptic tiling defects between the DA8 and DA9 neurons in unc-4(e26) mutant animals (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The unc-4(e26) mutation disrupts the physical interaction between UNC-4 and UNC-37.
source: To further test whether unc-4 and unc-37 function together in tiled synaptic innervation, we examined the synaptic tiling in unc-4(e26) mutants which carry a missense mutation in the eh1 domain that has been shown to disrupt the physical interaction between UNC-4 and UNC-37 (Winnier et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: UNC-4 and UNC-37 act together as a repressor complex for proper tiled synaptic innervation.
source: This result supports the idea that UNC-4 and UNC-37 act together as a repressor complex for proper tiled synaptic innervation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that unc-4(e26) mutants have synaptic tiling defects.

claim: Semaphorin–Plexin signaling controls the synaptic tiling of DA8 and DA9.
source: We have previously shown that Semaphorin (Sema)–Plexin signaling controls the synaptic tiling of DA8 and DA9 (Chen et al., 2018; Mizumoto and Shen, 2013a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: In the loss of function mutants of smp-1/Sema, plx-1/Plexin, and rap-2/Rap2A, DA8 and DA9 show severe synaptic tiling defects.
source: In the loss of function mutants of smp-1/Sema, plx-1/Plexin, and rap-2/Rap2A, DA8 and DA9 show severe synaptic tiling defects (Chen et al., 2018; Mizumoto and Shen, 2013a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: plx-1 mutants did not enhance the synaptic tiling defects of unc-4 or unc-37 mutants.
source: Consistent with this idea, plx-1 mutants did not enhance the synaptic tiling defects of unc-4 or unc-37 mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–D.

claim: unc-4 and unc-37 may function in the same genetic pathway as plx-1.
source: This result suggests that both unc-4 and unc-37 may function in the same genetic pathway as plx-1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic interaction data.

claim: PLX-1::GFP is localized at the anterior edge of the DA9 synaptic domain where it locally inhibits synapse formation in a smp-1-dependent manner.
source: We have previously shown that PLX-1::GFP is localized at the anterior edge of the DA9 synaptic domain where it locally inhibits synapse formation in a smp-1-dependent manner (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E; Mizumoto and Shen, 2013a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 3E.

claim: In unc-37 mutants, PLX-1::GFP localization was unaffected.
source: In unc-37 mutants, PLX-1::GFP localization was unaffected (Figure 1—figure supplement 3G), suggesting that smp-1 functions properly in the absence of unc-37.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3G.

claim: In unc-4(e2322ts) mutants, PLX-1::GFP localization was normal.
source: We observed normal PLX-1::GFP localization in the DA9 axon (Figure 1—figure supplement 3F), suggesting that smp-1 also functions properly in unc-4 mutants.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3F.

claim: There is a minor reduction in plx-1 expression in unc-37 mutants.
source: We then tested the possible functions of unc-4 and unc-37 on plx-1 expression using a Pplx-1::GFP transcription reporter and found a minor reduction in plx-1 expression in unc-37 mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–D.

claim: The subtle reduction in plx-1 expression is unlikely to explain the complete penetrant synaptic tiling defect of unc-4 and unc-37 mutants.
source: However, this subtle reduction in plx-1 expression is unlikely to explain the complete penetrant synaptic tiling defect of unc-4 and unc-37 mutants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of the penetrance of plx-1 expression defects and synaptic tiling defects.

claim: Expression of plx-1 cDNA under the DA-neuron-specific promoter did not rescue the synaptic tiling defects of unc-4 or unc-37 mutants.
source: Furthermore, expression of plx-1 cDNA under the DA-neuron-specific promoter (Punc-4c) did not rescue the synaptic tiling defects of unc-4 or unc-37 mutants (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data mentioned in the text.

claim: Ectopic synapse formation anterior to the PLX-1::GFP domain was observed in unc-4 and unc-37 mutants.
source: While PLX-1::GFP localization was not affected in unc-4 and unc-37 mutants, we observed the ectopic synapse formation anterior to the PLX-1::GFP domain (Figure 1—figure supplement 3F and G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3F and G.

claim: There was no reduction in rap-2 expression in unc-4 and unc-37 mutants.
source: However, we did not observe a reduction in rap-2 expression in unc-4 and unc-37 mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 4E–H), and the expression of known Sema/Plexin signaling components (rap-2 and mig-15) under the DA neuron-specific promoter (Punc-4c) did not rescue the synaptic tiling defects of unc-4 and unc-37 mutants (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4E–H.

claim: unc-4 and unc-37 may regulate synaptic tiling by controlling the expression of previously uncharacterized Sema–Plexin signaling components.
source: It is therefore possible that unc-4 and unc-37 regulate synaptic tiling by controlling the expression of previously uncharacterized Sema–Plexin signaling components.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental observations.

claim: The expression of Punc-53 (DA cell fate marker) was not affected in both anterior and posterior DA8/9 neurons in unc-4 and unc-37 mutants.
source: In the unc-4(e120) and unc-37(e262) mutant animals, the expression of Punc-53 was not affected in both anterior and posterior DA8/9 neurons, suggesting that DA8 and DA9 retain A-type identity (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: The expression of Punc-129DB in DA8/9 of unc-4 and unc-37 mutants was not different from wild type.
source: The expression of a DB marker Punc-129DB in DA8/9 of unc-4 and unc-37 mutants was not different from wild type, while there was a slight increase in the number of animals expressing the other DB markers, Pacr-16 and Pacr-5, with a slightly higher penetrance in the posterior DA8/9 (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: There was a slight increase in the number of animals expressing Pacr-16 and Pacr-5 in DA8/9 of unc-4 and unc-37 mutants.
source: The expression of a DB marker Punc-129DB in DA8/9 of unc-4 and unc-37 mutants was not different from wild type, while there was a slight increase in the number of animals expressing the other DB markers, Pacr-16 and Pacr-5, with a slightly higher penetrance in the posterior DA8/9 (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: DA8 and DA9 might have minor cell fate defects that result in the leaky expression of some DB markers.
source: These results suggest that DA8 and DA9 might have minor cell fate defects that result in the leaky expression of some DB markers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing slight increase in DB marker expression.

claim: The low penetrance of the partial cell fate defects is less likely to account for the fully penetrant synaptic tiling defects of unc-4 and unc-37 mutants.
source: However, the low penetrance of the partial cell fate defects is less likely to account for the fully penetrant synaptic tiling defects of unc-4 and unc-37 mutants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of penetrance of cell fate defects and synaptic tiling defects.

claim: DA9-specific markers Pmig-13, Pglr-4, and Pitr-1 were expressed in DA9 of wild-type animals at full penetrance.
source: These DA9 markers were expressed in DA9 of wild-type animals at full penetrance (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: In unc-4 mutants, Pglr-4 and Pmig-13 were expressed in DA9, while Pmig-13 expression was noticeably weaker than wild type.
source: In all unc-4 mutants, we observed expression of Pglr-4 and Pmig-13, while Pmig-13 expression was noticeably weaker than wild type as described above (Table 1 and Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1 and Figure 1C.

claim: In unc-37 mutant animals, the expression of DA9 specific markers was mostly unaffected, with a small fraction of animals lacking Pglr-4 expression in DA9.
source: In unc-37 mutant animals, the expression of these DA9 specific markers was mostly unaffected, with a small fraction of animals (7/100) lacking Pglr-4 expression in DA9 (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: The cell fates of DA8 and DA9 in unc-4 and unc-37 mutants are largely unaffected.
source: Together we conclude that despite the subtle changes in the expression of some of the cell fate markers, the cell fates of DA8 and DA9 in unc-4 and unc-37 mutants are largely unaffected, and therefore, it is unlikely that the synaptic tiling defects of unc-4 and unc-37 mutants are due to the secondary defects of cell fate transformation of the DA neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data on cell fate marker expression.

claim: DA-specific continuous degradation of UNC-4 and UNC-37 resulted in severe synaptic tiling defects.
source: Using this system, we first conducted the DA-specific continuous degradation of UNC-4 and UNC-37 by placing the L4 parental animals on K-NAA-containing plates and observing the progeny at the L4 stage. We observed severe synaptic tiling defects between the DA8 and DA9 synaptic domains (Figure 2B, D, and E), suggesting that unc-4 and unc-37 are required in the DA neurons for proper synaptic tiling.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B, D, and E.

claim: unc-4 and unc-37 are required in the DA neurons for proper synaptic tiling.
source: We observed severe synaptic tiling defects between the DA8 and DA9 synaptic domains (Figure 2B, D, and E), suggesting that unc-4 and unc-37 are required in the DA neurons for proper synaptic tiling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data from DA-specific degradation experiments.

claim: Expression of unc-4 in both DA8 and DA9 neurons significantly rescued the synaptic tiling defect in unc-4 mutant animals.
source: We observed significant rescue of the synaptic tiling defect when unc-4 is expressed in both DA8 and DA9 neurons of unc-4 mutant animals (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Expression of unc-37 in both DA8 and DA9 neurons significantly rescued the synaptic tiling defects in unc-37 mutant animals.
source: Similarly, we observed significant rescue of the synaptic tiling defects in unc-37 mutant animals when unc-37 is expressed in both DA8 and DA9 neurons (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Expression of unc-4 or unc-37 only in DA9 did not rescue the synaptic tiling defects.
source: However, in the genetic mosaic animals in which unc-4 or unc-37 is expressed only in DA9, we did not observe rescue of the synaptic tiling defects (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F and G.

claim: unc-4 and unc-37 are not sufficient in DA9 and instead function in both DA8 and DA9 neurons to control synaptic tiling.
source: This suggests that unc-4 and unc-37 are not sufficient in DA9 and instead function in both DA8 and DA9 neurons to control synaptic tiling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mosaic rescue experiments.

claim: The DA neurons are born in the late gastrulation stage and complete development during late embryogenesis.
source: The DA neurons are born in the late gastrulation stage and completes the development during late embryogenesis (Sulston et al., 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The tiled synaptic innervation of DA8 and DA9 is observed at the early first larval (L1) stage in wild-type animals.
source: The tiled synaptic innervation of DA8 and DA9 is observed at the early first larval (L1) stage in wild-type animals (Mizumoto and Shen, 2013a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: unc-4(e2322ts) mutants carry a point mutation (L121F) that resides in the homeodomain.
source: unc-4(e2322ts) mutants carry a point mutation (L121F) that resides in the homeodomain (Winnier et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The unc-4(e2322ts) mutation is permissive at 16°C and restrictive at 25°C.
source: The unc-4(e2322ts) mutation is permissive at 16°C and restrictive at 25°C (Miller et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: unc-4(e2322ts) mutants grown at 16°C did not exhibit synaptic tiling defects.
source: When grown at the permissive temperature (16°C), unc-4(e2322ts) mutants did not exhibit synaptic tiling defects compared with wild type (Figure 3B,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and F.

claim: unc-4(e2322ts) mutants grown at 25°C showed severe synaptic tiling defects.
source: When grown at the restrictive temperature (25°C), unc-4(e2322ts) mutants showed severe synaptic tiling defects (Figure 3C,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and F.

claim: Embryonic knockdown of unc-4 by down-shifting the growth temperature from 25°C to 16°C at the L1 stage did not result in significant synaptic tiling defects.
source: Interestingly, we did not observe significant synaptic tiling defects when unc-4 was knocked down embryonically by down-shifting the growth temperature of unc-4(e2322ts) mutant animals from 25°C to 16°C at the L1 stage (Figure 3D,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and F.

claim: unc-4 is not required for synaptic tiling during the embryonic stage when the DA8 and DA9 cell fates are determined.
source: This result indicates that unc-4 is not required for synaptic tiling during the embryonic stage when the DA8 and DA9 cell fates are determined by unc-4.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temperature shift experiment results.

claim: Postembryonic unc-4 knockdown by up-shifting the growth temperature from 16°C to 25°C at the L1 stage resulted in severe synaptic tiling defects.
source: Conversely, the postembryonic unc-4 knockdown by up-shifting the growth temperature from 16°C to 25°C at the L1 stage resulted in severe synaptic tiling defects (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: unc-4 is required in the postmitotic DA8 and DA9 neurons in which the cell fates are already set.
source: Together, this suggests that unc-4 is required in the postmitotic DA8 and DA9 neurons in which the cell fates are already set.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temperature shift experiment results.

claim: Embryonic degradation of UNC-4 in DA neurons did not result in synaptic tiling defects.
source: Consistent with the temperature shift experiments using unc-4(e2322ts) mutants, we did not observe any synaptic tiling defects when UNC-4 was degraded during embryonic development (Figure 4B,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and F.

claim: Embryonic degradation of UNC-37 resulted in severe synaptic tiling defects.
source: On the other hand, embryonic degradation of UNC-37 resulted in severe synaptic tiling defects (Figure 4C,F), suggesting that UNC-37 but not UNC-4 is required during embryonic development to regulate synaptic tiling.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and F.

claim: UNC-37 but not UNC-4 is required during embryonic development to regulate synaptic tiling.
source: On the other hand, embryonic degradation of UNC-37 resulted in severe synaptic tiling defects (Figure 4C,F), suggesting that UNC-37 but not UNC-4 is required during embryonic development to regulate synaptic tiling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the embryonic degradation experiments.

claim: Synaptic tiling between DA8 and DA9 is observed as early as L1 stage.
source: We have previously shown that synaptic tiling between DA8 and DA9 is observed as early as L1 stage (Mizumoto and Shen, 2013a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Embryonic degradation of UNC-37 but not UNC-4 caused synaptic tiling defects at early L2 stage.
source: We found that embryonic degradation of UNC-37 but not UNC-4 caused synaptic tiling defects (Figures 4D, E, and G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4D, E, and G.

claim: unc-4 is not required to establish the synaptic tiling.
source: Our results suggest that unc-4 is not required to establish the synaptic tiling, whereas unc-37 may be required to establish the synaptic tiling during embryonic development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the embryonic degradation experiments examined at L2 stage.

claim: unc-37 may be required to establish the synaptic tiling during embryonic development.
source: Our results suggest that unc-4 is not required to establish the synaptic tiling, whereas unc-37 may be required to establish the synaptic tiling during embryonic development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the embryonic degradation experiments examined at L2 stage.

claim: Postembryonic degradation of UNC-4 resulted in synaptic tiling defects comparable to continuous UNC-4 degradation.
source: Consistent with our findings using the temperature-sensitive mutant of unc-4, we found that postembryonic degradation of UNC-4 resulted in synaptic tiling defects, which were comparable to the continuous UNC-4 degradation (Figure 5B,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and F.

claim: unc-4 is exclusively required in the postmitotic DA neurons to regulate synaptic tiling.
source: Together with the lack of synaptic tiling defects after embryonic degradation of UNC-4, these data suggest that unc-4 is exclusively required in the postmitotic DA neurons to regulate synaptic tiling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the postembryonic and embryonic degradation experiments.

claim: Postembryonic degradation of UNC-37 resulted in severe synaptic tiling defects.
source: Similar to unc-4, postembryonic degradation of UNC-37 resulted in severe synaptic tiling defects (Figure 5C,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and F.

claim: unc-37 is required for the synaptic tiling during DA neurogenesis as well as in the postmitotic DA neurons.
source: This suggests that, unlike unc-4, unc-37 is required for the synaptic tiling during DA neurogenesis as well as in the postmitotic DA neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the postembryonic and embryonic degradation experiments.

claim: unc-37 may function with other transcription factors during DA neurogenesis for synaptic tiling.
source: Given that unc-4 is specifically required in the postmitotic DA neurons, this result suggests that unc-37 may function with other transcription factors during DA neurogenesis for synaptic tiling (Figure 7).
evidence: This is speculation based on the differential temporal requirements of unc-4 and unc-37.

claim: Degradation of UNC-4 and UNC-37 after mid-L2 stage caused mild yet significant synaptic tiling defects.
source: We found that degradation of UNC-4 and UNC-37 after mid-L2 stage caused mild yet significant synaptic tiling defects (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D–F.

claim: unc-4 and unc-37 are required throughout postembryonic development for the maintenance of the synaptic tiling.
source: Weaker synaptic tiling defects in the late postembryonic degradation of UNC-4 and UNC-37 suggest that unc-4 and unc-37 are required throughout postembryonic development for the maintenance of the synaptic tiling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the late postembryonic degradation experiments.

claim: unc-4 and unc-37 repress the expression of ceh-12 in the VA motor neurons to specify the AVA>VA synaptic connections.
source: It has been shown that unc-4 and unc-37 repress the expression of ceh-12, a member of the HB9 family of Homeobox genes, in the VA motor neurons to specify the AVA>VA synaptic connections (Von Stetina et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Loss of ceh-12 partially restores the synaptic input and locomotion defects of unc-4 and unc-37 mutants.
source: Loss of ceh-12 partially restores the synaptic input and locomotion defects of unc-4 and unc-37 mutants (Von Stetina et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Ectopic expression of ceh-12 in VA neurons is sufficient to induce unc-4 mutant-like uncoordinated locomotion phenotype.
source: Furthermore, the ectopic expression of ceh-12 in VA neurons is sufficient to induce unc-4 mutant-like uncoordinated locomotion phenotype (Von Stetina et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Pceh-12::GFP expression was not detected in DA8 and DA9 of wild type at L1, L2, or L4 stage.
source: Pceh-12::GFP expression was not detected in DA8 and DA9 of wild type at L1, L2, or L4 stage (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–A").
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–A".

claim: Weak ectopic expression of Pceh-12::GFP in DA8 and DA9 neurons was observed at L2 and L4 stage in unc-4 and unc-37 mutants.
source: We observed weak ectopic expression of Pceh-12::GFP in DA8 and DA9 neurons at L2 and L4 stage in unc-4 and unc-37 mutants (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B'–B" and C'-C').
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B'–B" and C'-C'.

claim: At the L1 stage, ectopic Pceh-12::GFP expression in DA8 and DA9 was only detected in unc-37 but not in unc-4 mutants.
source: However, at the L1 stage, the ectopic Pceh-12::GFP expression in DA8 and DA9 was only detected in unc-37 but not in unc-4 mutants (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Expression of ceh-12 cDNA in DA neurons caused significant synaptic tiling defects in wild-type animals.
source: To test whether the ectopic expression of ceh-12 in the DA neurons underlies the synaptic tiling defects of unc-4 and unc-37, we expressed ceh-12 cDNA using the DA neuron-specific promoter (Punc-4c) in wild-type animals. We observed significant synaptic tiling defects in these animals (Figure 6A,C), suggesting that unc-4 and unc-37 likely repress the expression of ceh-12 in DA neurons for proper synaptic tiling.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and C.

claim: unc-4 and unc-37 likely repress the expression of ceh-12 in DA neurons for proper synaptic tiling.
source: We observed significant synaptic tiling defects in these animals (Figure 6A,C), suggesting that unc-4 and unc-37 likely repress the expression of ceh-12 in DA neurons for proper synaptic tiling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ectopic expression experiment.

claim: Ectopic expression of unc-55 in DA neurons did not cause synaptic tiling defects.
source: Ectopic expression of unc-55 in DA neurons did not cause synaptic tiling defects (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: ceh-12 mutation did not suppress the synaptic tiling defects of unc-4 and unc-37 mutants.
source: While these results strongly suggest that ceh-12 functions downstream of unc-4 and unc-37 in synaptic tiling, ceh-12 mutation did not suppress the synaptic tiling defects of unc-4 and unc-37 mutants (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The weak ectopic expression of ceh-12 in unc-4 and unc-37 mutants is not sufficient to cause the synaptic tiling defects.
source: This suggests that the weak ectopic expression of ceh-12 in unc-4 and unc-37 mutants is not sufficient to cause the synaptic tiling defects, and there are additional factor(s) that function redundantly with ceh-12 under the control of unc-4 and unc-37 in synaptic tiling (Figure 7).
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of suppression by ceh-12 mutation.

claim: There are additional factor(s) that function redundantly with ceh-12 under the control of unc-4 and unc-37 in synaptic tiling.
source: This suggests that the weak ectopic expression of ceh-12 in unc-4 and unc-37 mutants is not sufficient to cause the synaptic tiling defects, and there are additional factor(s) that function redundantly with ceh-12 under the control of unc-4 and unc-37 in synaptic tiling (Figure 7).
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental observations.

claim: EGL-20 acts through the canonical Wnt signaling pathway components including bar-1/β-catenin to positively regulate the expression of ceh-12 in VA motor neurons.
source: Previous work has shown that EGL-20, a Wnt morphogen that is expressed in the cells around the preanal ganglion (Whangbo and Kenyon, 1999), acts through the canonical Wnt signaling pathway components including bar-1/β-catenin, to positively regulate the expression of ceh-12 in VA motor neurons (Schneider et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: unc-4 and unc-37 inhibit the expression of ceh-12 by repressing the expression of the Frizzled receptors, mom-5 and mig-1.
source: unc-4 and unc-37 inhibits the expression of ceh-12 by repressing the expression of the Frizzled receptors, mom-5 and mig-1 (Schneider et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: bar-1(ga80) partially suppressed the synaptic tiling defect of unc-4 and unc-37 mutants.
source: Consistent with our idea, bar-1(ga80) partially suppressed the synaptic tiling defect of unc-4 and unc-37 mutants (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: UNC-4 and UNC-37 control synaptic tiling by inhibiting the canonical Wnt signaling for the expression of multiple genes including ceh-12.
source: This result suggests that UNC-4 and UNC-37 control synaptic tiling by inhibiting the canonical Wnt signaling for the expression of multiple genes including ceh-12.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic interaction with bar-1.

claim: Sustained expression of neuronal cell fate determinants in differentiated neurons is required to maintain effector gene expression for the functionality of neurons.
source: Previous studies in both vertebrate and invertebrate systems have demonstrated that sustained expression of neuronal cell fate determinants in the differentiated neurons is required to maintain effector gene expression for the functionality of neurons (Altun-Gultekin et al., 2001; Carney et al., 2013; Cheng et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Sustained expression of Nurr1 is required for the survival of the midbrain dopaminergic neurons and maintained expression of genes required for dopamine synthesis and transport.
source: For example, sustained expression of Nurr1 is required for the survival of the midbrain dopaminergic neurons and maintained expression of the genes required for dopamine synthesis and transport (Kadkhodaei et al., 2009; Saucedo-Cardenas et al., 1998; Zetterström et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The AID system is an effective method to uncover the novel spatiotemporal functions of well-characterized genes.
source: Our work also highlights that the AID system is an effective method to uncover the novel spatiotemporal functions of well-characterized genes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the successful use of the AID system in this study.

claim: Recent work using the AID system showed that unc-86/Brn3a is required for both the initiation and maintenance of multiple neuronal identities in C. elegans.
source: Indeed, recent work using the AID system showed that the BRN3-type POU homeobox gene unc-86/Brn3a is required for both the initiation and maintenance of multiple neuronal identities in C. elegans (Serrano-Saiz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The combination of CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing technologies and the AID system will allow examination of the spatiotemporal functions of any genes, including genes whose null mutants are lethal.
source: The combination of CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing technologies and the AID system will allow us to examine the spatiotemporal functions of any genes, including the genes whose null mutants are lethal.
evidence: This is speculation about future applications of the technology.

claim: Neuronal cell fate transformations often lead to altered synaptic connectivity.
source: Neuronal cell fate transformations often lead to altered synaptic connectivity.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by subsequent examples in the text.

claim: The temporal transcription factor Hunchback in Drosophila controls the neuroblast lineage NB7-1 that gives rise to U1-5 motor neurons.
source: The temporal transcription factor Hunchback in Drosophila controls the neuroblast lineage NB7-1 that gives rise to the U1-5 motor neurons which innervate the dorsal (U1-2) and ventral (U3-5) muscles (Isshiki et al., 2001; Kohwi and Doe, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Perturbed expression of Hunchback in the NB7-1 lineage results in the serial formation of U1 neurons, all of which project to the dorsal muscles.
source: Perturbed expression of Hunchback in the NB7-1 lineage results in the serial formation of U1 neurons, all of which project to the dorsal muscles (Isshiki et al., 2001; Pearson and Doe, 2003; Seroka and Doe, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: unc-4 and unc-37 mutants exhibit synaptic specificity defects in the VA motor neurons due to the partial cell fate transformation of the VA neurons to VB neurons.
source: Likewise, unc-4 and unc-37 mutants exhibit synaptic specificity defects in the VA motor neurons due to the partial cell fate transformation of the VA neurons to VB neurons (Miller et al., 1992; White et al., 1992; Winnier et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Drosophila Unc-4 is required in the 7B neurons for the projections into the ipsilateral and contralateral leg neuropils.
source: Similarly, Drosophila Unc-4 is required in the 7B neurons for the projections into the ipsilateral and contralateral leg neuropils (Lacin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The miswiring phenotype of Drosophila Unc-4 is likely due to cell fate transformation because Unc-4 is specifically required during development.
source: This miswiring phenotype is also likely due to the cell fate transformation because Unc-4 is specifically required during development (Lacin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference based on citation to previous literature.

claim: The presynaptic patterning defects in the mutants of cell fate determinants could occur independent of the cell fate transformation.
source: Our data therefore suggest that the synaptic patterning defects in the mutants of cell fate determinants could occur independent of the cell fate transformation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings of this study.

claim: The mechanisms of the DA8 and DA9 cell fate specification may be slightly distinct from the anterior DA neurons.
source: One possible explanation is that the mechanisms of the DA8 and DA9 cell fate specification is slightly distinct from the anterior DA neurons.
evidence: This is speculation to explain the lack of cell fate defects in DA8 and DA9 of unc-4 and unc-37 mutants.

claim: DA9 has distinct gene expression profiles compared with the other DA neurons.
source: Consistently, these two most posterior DA neurons, especially DA9, have distinct gene expression profiles compared with the other DA neurons, as exemplified by the series of DA9-specific markers (Kratsios et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: VA neurons exert tiled synaptic innervation.
source: Similar to DA neurons, VA neurons also exert tiled synaptic innervation (White et al., 1976).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: unc-4 and unc-37 play crucial roles in the AVA>VA wiring specificity primarily during the development of VA neurons.
source: Because unc-4 and unc-37 have been shown to play crucial roles in the AVA>VA wiring specificity primarily during the development of VA neurons (Miller et al., 1992; Winnier et al., 1999), it would be interesting to examine if unc-4 and unc-37 also play a role in VA synaptic tiling.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The potential role for unc-4 in the maintenance of AVA>VA synaptic connection in the L2–L3 stage is consistent with the discovery of the post-mitotic functions of unc-4 and unc-37 in precise neuronal pattern formation.
source: Nevertheless, the potential role for unc-4 in the maintenance of AVA>VA synaptic connection in the L2–L3 stage (Miller et al., 1992) is consistent with our discovery of the post-mitotic functions of unc-4 and unc-37 in precise neuronal pattern formation.
evidence: This is an inference connecting previous observations with the current findings.

claim: The tiled synaptic pattern of DA8 and DA9 is solely dependent on the physical interaction between the axons of DA8 and DA9 which is mediated by Semaphorin–Plexin signaling.
source: Previously, we showed that the tiled synaptic pattern of DA8 and DA9 is solely dependent on the physical interaction between the axons of DA8 and DA9 which is mediated by Semaphorin–Plexin signaling (Mizumoto and Shen, 2013a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The positions of DA8 and DA9 synapses are determined by the Wnt gradient cues rather than the position of the post-synaptic muscle cells.
source: We also showed that the positions of DA8 and DA9 synapses are determined by the Wnt gradient cues rather than the position of the post-synaptic muscle cells (Klassen and Shen, 2007; Mizumoto and Shen, 2013b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: It is unlikely that the synaptic tiling defects observed in unc-4 and unc-37 mutants are the synaptic specificity defects between the DA neurons and the post-synaptic muscle cells.
source: Therefore, it is unlikely that the synaptic tiling defects we observed in unc-4 and unc-37 mutants are the synaptic specificity defects between the DA neurons and the post-synaptic muscle cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on previous findings about the mechanisms of synaptic tiling.

claim: The Groucho family of transcriptional corepressors are known to function with various transcription factors during animal development.
source: The Groucho family of transcriptional corepressors are known to function with various transcription factors during animal development (Gasperowicz and Otto, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: UNC-37 interacts with eh1 domain-containing homeobox proteins (COG-1 and MAB-9) and POP-1/T-cell factor to regulate cell fate specifications during development.
source: In addition to UNC-4, UNC-37 interacts with eh1 domain-containing homeobox proteins (COG-1 and MAB-9) (Chang et al., 2003; Jafari et al., 2011; Winnier et al., 1999) and POP-1/T-cell factor (Calvo et al., 2001) to regulate cell fate specifications during development.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: UNC-4 inhibits canonical Wnt signaling to repress ceh-12 expression in VA neurons.
source: UNC-4 inhibits canonical Wnt signaling to repress ceh-12 expression in VA neurons (Schneider et al., 2012; Von Stetina et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Loss of egl-20/wnt or mig-1/frizzled in unc-4 mutants suppresses the ectopic expression of ceh-12 in the VA neurons and restores the VA-AVA connections.
source: Consistently, loss of egl-20/wnt or mig-1/frizzled in unc-4 mutants suppresses the ectopic expression of ceh-12 in the VA neurons and restores the VA-AVA connections (Schneider et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: ceh-12 is not the only Wnt effector gene that regulates synaptic tiling and is upregulated in the unc-4 and unc-37 mutants.
source: This suggests that ceh-12 is not the only Wnt effector gene that regulates synaptic tiling and is upregulated in the unc-4 and unc-37 mutants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of suppression by ceh-12 mutation.

claim: The canonical Wnt signaling pathway is required for the proper tiled synaptic innervation in the DA neurons.
source: The genetic interaction between bar-1 and unc-4 (and unc-37) indicates that the canonical Wnt signaling pathway is required for the proper tiled synaptic innervation in the DA neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic interaction data.

claim: Wnt signaling functions as a negative regulator of synaptic tiling which is controlled by Sema–Plexin signaling.
source: Specifically, Wnt signaling functions as a negative regulator of synaptic tiling (Figure 7) which is controlled by Sema–Plexin signaling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic interaction data and the model shown in Figure 7.

claim: Sema–Plexin signaling functions as a negative regulator of synapse formation in both C. elegans and mice.
source: Sema–Plexin signaling has been shown to function as a negative regulator of synapse formation in both C. elegans and mice (Duan et al., 2014; Mizumoto and Shen, 2013a; Tran et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Wnt signaling may function as a prosynaptogenic cue by inhibiting Sema/Plexin signaling.
source: It is therefore possible that Wnt signaling functions as a prosynaptogenic cue by inhibiting Sema/Plexin signaling.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known functions of Sema/Plexin signaling.

claim: Wnt-7a has been shown to induce synaptogenesis.
source: Indeed, Wnt-7a has been shown to induce synaptogenesis (Hall et al., 2000; Lucas and Salinas, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Two Wnts, LIN-44 and EGL-20, function as gradient inhibitory cues for the proper positioning of DA8 and DA9 synapses.
source: In addition to the function of canonical Wnt signaling in synaptic tiling, we and others have shown that two Wnts, LIN-44 and EGL-20, function as gradient inhibitory cues for the proper positioning of DA8 and DA9 synapses (Klassen and Shen, 2007; Mizumoto and Shen, 2013b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: Disruption of the Wnt gradient patterns affect the severity of the synaptic tiling defects of plx-1 mutants, due to the displaced synapse position of DA8 and DA9.
source: Disruption of the Wnt gradient patterns affect the severity of the synaptic tiling defects of plx-1 mutants, due to the displaced synapse position of DA8 and DA9 (Mizumoto and Shen, 2013b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: egl-20 enhances the synaptic tiling defects of plx-1 mutants due to the posterior displacement of the DA8 synaptic domain.
source: For example, egl-20 enhances the synaptic tiling defects of plx-1 mutants due to the posterior displacement of the DA8 synaptic domain.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The function of Wnt gradient signal in synapse positioning is mediated by previously uncharacterized non-canonical pathways as it does not require canonical Wnt pathway components including bar-1/β-catenin.
source: The function of Wnt gradient signal in synapse positioning is mediated by previously uncharacterized non-canonical pathways as it does not require canonical Wnt pathway components including bar-1/β-catenin (Klassen and Shen, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Canonical Wnt signaling and non-canonical Wnt signaling cooperatively regulate the precise synapse patterning in C. elegans.
source: Our results therefore suggest that canonical Wnt signaling and non-canonical Wnt signaling cooperatively regulate the precise synapse patterning in C. elegans.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings of this study and previous work.
